Kanawha County and how the tax is organized

Charleston, the state capital, is the seat of Kanawha County. Besides Charleston, the county holds Dunbar, Marmet, St. Albans and South Charleston, plus parts of Nitro, Montgomery and Smithers. Smaller towns such as Belle, Cedar Grove, Clendenin and Pratt sit along the river valleys.

The county runs on four magisterial districts. Where your house sits decides whether the municipal levy applies to it, and that changes the bill. For the 2025 tax year the county purposes levy is $70,942,064, and $21,188,680 of it comes from voter-approved excess levies.

The assessor is at 409 Virginia Street E., Charleston. If you move, send the new address to the Assessor's Office. The sheriff does not change it.

How the sheriff bills and collects

The Sheriff's Tax Office mails statements by July 15 each year, and the sheriff, not the assessor, collects the money. Statements reflect ownership as of the prior July 1. The office says taxpayers avoid interest by paying the first half before October 1 and the second half by April 1. The state calendar also lists September 1 and March 1 as the installment dates that earn the 2.5 percent discount.

Payments can be made several ways. The office accepts Visa, Mastercard and Discover by phone during business hours, and you need the eight digit account number printed in small type at the top right of your statement. Mailed checks go to 409 Virginia St E, Room 120, Charleston, WV 25301, with the account number on the memo line.

  • Personal property bills run a year behind, so a vehicle you sold can still appear on a statement.
  • Lost statements can be replaced by phone, and an online tax inquiry link is on the sheriff's website.

A statement that never reached a vacant or inherited house is still a debt. Run the online inquiry before listing or signing with a buyer.

When real estate tax goes unpaid

Unpaid tax first turns into interest at 9 percent a year, and later into a tax lien that can be sold. State rules mark October 1 as the delinquency date for the first half and April 1 for the second. The sheriff's collection page says about 100,000 tickets exist at the start of a year and that roughly 92 percent of current-year tax is collected within the first 10 months.

Delinquent real estate liens are now sold through the State Auditor after a change in state law, so ask the Sheriff's Tax Office who runs the sale for your parcel and what the redemption steps are.

The collection unit also tracks bad checks, bankruptcy claims and the county hotel and motel tax. A homeowner who is behind on tax and also in bankruptcy should expect the office to file a claim.

How to challenge an assessment

Your protest goes to the county commission, wearing its Board of Equalization and Review hat from February 1 until the end of that month. Once its work is finished the board can close after February 15. Owners who let the window pass generally lose the right to question that year's list, unless they appeal to the Office of Tax Appeals.

Value is the board's subject, not what kind of property it is. When a parcel sits above or below 60 percent of true and actual value, the board resets it to 60 percent, and any increase requires five days of written notice. Disputes over class or taxability belong with the assessor first, then the Tax Commissioner. An owner-occupied house wrongly sitting in Class IV is one of those classification disputes.

  • To fight the board's order, file with the Office of Tax Appeals before March 31 of the tax year.
  • You carry the burden, and a preponderance of the evidence is enough.
  • Recent sale prices, repair estimates and photos of defects are the usual evidence.

Flood history and condition problems

The June 2016 flood left a long mark on the county's river-valley neighborhoods. On June 23, 2016, heavy thunderstorms caused flash flooding across West Virginia, including in Clendenin and Elkview, where a bridge collapsed. The Kanawha River forms at Gauley Bridge and is joined by the Elk River in Charleston.

If you own a house that took water, still has damaged floors or has a roof and furnace that need work, you face a decision. Repairing and listing on the open market takes time and cash, and a buyer's lender may balk at condition. A cash buyer who purchases as-is lets you skip that repair cycle, and you still settle taxes from the proceeds.

Taxes and costs when you sell

Expect to settle delinquent property tax, a transfer tax and any liens out of the proceeds. Recording a deed triggers a state excise tax, and the statute adds a county excise tax at 55 cents per $500 of value. A transfer worth $1,000 or less does not count as a taxable document.

The regular ceiling for an owner-occupied Class II home inside a municipality adds up to $1.00 per $100 of assessed value, made up of 0.50 cents for the state, 28.60 for the county, 45.90 for schools and 25.00 for the municipality, all in cents per $100. Kanawha County carries an excess levy, so the real figure can run higher. Rental and vacant property can fall in Class III or IV, where ceilings are higher.

  • Homeowners who are 65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled, can exempt $20,000 of assessed value.
  • The exemption needs West Virginia residency for the two prior calendar years.
  • Before the closing date, have the title company pull a payoff on any open ticket.

Steps for selling with a balance owed

Sellers with open tax can follow a short sequence. Call 304-357-0210 or use the online inquiry to see which halves are unpaid for the current and earlier years. Gather the account number from the top right of a statement, or ask the office to look the parcel up. Next, tell the title company what you found so the payoff is built into the closing figures. If the house is a rental or has an occupant, tell the title agent that as well, since the Class III or Class IV rate may apply.

Timing helps. A closing before the next delinquency date keeps interest from growing, and a payoff request made a few days before the closing keeps the number accurate.

Selling with tax due, repairs or tenants

Most sellers we hear from in Kanawha County are not pricing a perfect home. Their situations are an inherited house in Charleston, a St. Albans rental whose tenant will not leave, or a parcel with tickets in arrears. Our purchases are as-is and for cash. The tax gets paid at the closing table, and cleaning out, repairs and staging are off your list. Reach us at (424) 435-2326 for a written offer to weigh against any other.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Kanawha County tax due dates?

Installments fall on September 1 and March 1, and paying ahead of either earns a 2.5 percent discount. The sheriff's office advises paying the first half before October 1 and the second by April 1 to stay clear of interest.

How much interest does Kanawha County charge on late tax?

Interest on late tax is 9 percent per year. It starts after October 1 for the first half and after April 1 for the second.

Who do I call about a Kanawha County tax bill?

Bills and payments go through the Sheriff's Tax Office on 304-357-0210. For assessments and address changes, ring the Assessor's Office on 304-357-0250.

Can I sell a Kanawha County house if the taxes are unpaid?

Yes. Normally the closing pays what is owed out of your proceeds. Start by requesting a current payoff from the sheriff or the title company.

What is the deadline to protest a Kanawha County assessment?

Hearings before the commission as the Board of Equalization and Review begin February 1, and the board must adjourn by month's end. Further appeal to the Office of Tax Appeals is due by March 31.

Raleigh County at a glance

Raleigh County lies in southern West Virginia, with Beckley as its seat and its lone city. Census takers found 74,591 residents in 2020, and the 2025 estimate has slipped to 71,775 from a high of 96,273 in 1950. Coal drove that growth. Miners opened the seams in the 1890s, rails arrived in Beckley in 1901, and headcount leapt from 12,436 in 1900 to 25,633 in 1910.

The 1980s brought machines that replaced thousands of miners. Beckley coped better than the small camps, helped by its spot where Interstates 64 and 77 cross U.S. 19. Retail, services, tourism and hospitals carry the local economy now. Visitors come for the Exhibition Coal Mine, Grandview Park, Twin Falls State Park and the Winterplace ski resort, and part of New River Gorge National Park and Preserve lies inside the county line. Many sellers here own an older house, and plenty are heirs holding a property they never planned to manage.

Beyond Beckley you will find the towns of Lester, Mabscott and Sophia, and communities such as Shady Spring, Ghent and Piney View. Seven magisterial districts were merged into three in the 1970s. An old deed might name a district like Trap Hill that is no longer on any map, so hand that deed to the title company early.

Sheriff and assessor offices

Two desks share the work. Raleigh County's sheriff runs the Tax Division, which mails bills and takes money. The county assessor puts a value on each parcel and decides its class. A question about a ticket goes to the sheriff, and a question about your number goes to the assessor.

When staff runs thin, a satellite office may go dark for a day, so ring ahead before you head out to Ghent or Glen Daniel. Online payment and records links live on the Raleigh County Sheriff tax page and the Assessor's site.

Due dates and penalties

Raleigh County bills in two halves. Sheriffs mail tickets on or after July 15, and the halves fall due on September 1 and March 1, the same calendar used statewide.

  • Pay the first half by September 1. It turns delinquent on October 1.
  • Pay the second half by March 1. It turns delinquent on April 1.
  • Paying ahead of either due date earns a 2.5 percent discount on that half.
  • Late tax picks up interest at 9 percent a year.

Leaving a ticket unpaid can end in a lien sale. West Virginia Code 11A-3-2 has the sheriff build a second list by September 10 of parcels that were still unpaid on September 1. The State Auditor receives those certified liens on October 31. Before certification, an owner clears the debt with the sheriff by paying the tax, the interest and the charges: $25 for the list plus $10 for every mailed notice. Once certified, the Auditor handles redemption.

How a Raleigh County house is assessed

The assessor values your property at 60 percent of market value. Your rate then turns on the class the parcel falls in. A home that the owner owns and lives in, plus an owner-occupied farm, is Class II. Other property outside a municipality is Class III, and other property inside one is Class IV. Compared with Class I, Class II pays double and Classes III and IV pay four times as much.

Rentals and vacant inherited houses do not meet the Class II test. Find out your parcel's class before you list, since the class sets the bill your buyer steps into.

On where the money goes, tax year 2024 levies in the county split this way: schools 67.1 percent, county purposes 27.7 percent, municipal purposes 4.8 percent and state purposes 0.4 percent. Owner-occupied homes carry about 42 percent of the real estate levy.

How to appeal your assessment

Appeals are made in person, and the clock is short. Every winter the assessor lays out real estate and personal property assessments for public inspection, from late January into late February, and fixes have to be requested inside that stretch. Call the assessor for this year's exact dates.

West Virginia Code 11-3-24 turns the county commission into a review panel, the board of equalization and review. They convene by February 1, may adjourn once February 15 has gone by, and must be done at month's end. An owner who never asks that panel for relief forfeits a correction for that year, though the Office of Tax Appeals remains open. After a hearing, the board's order can be appealed there, and the owner must meet a preponderance of the evidence.

Classification and taxability are outside the board's reach. A house you believe sits in the wrong class goes to the assessor as a separate protest under section 11-3-24a.

Homestead exemption

This break is limited to owners 65 or older and to owners who are permanently and totally disabled. West Virginia Code 11-6B-3 shields the first $20,000 of assessed value on an owner-occupied homestead, and the owner needs two years of state residency.

The home you lived in on the July 1 assessment date is the one that counts, and the savings begin the next tax year. A transfer by deed, will or any other route ends the break on the following July 1, unless the new owner meets the same tests. The assessor's site also links a Disabled Veteran Real Property Tax Credit form.

Selling with taxes owed

Back taxes will not block a closing, yet they must be settled before the deed is recorded. Here is the order that tends to work:

  • Have the sheriff's tax staff report on each ticket for the parcel, earlier years too.
  • Learn from the title company if the second list or a lien sale reaches the property.
  • Settle the balance from the sale check or ahead of closing, so no lien rides along with the deed.
  • Record the deed at the clerk's office and pay the transfer tax.

The transfer tax comes from West Virginia Code 11-22-2. It is $1.10 for each $500 of value, now retained by the county. A second county levy adds 55 cents per $500 unless the county raised it, and a $20 fee applies when the transfer is for consideration. The seller, as grantor, pays unless the buyer takes the deed with the tax still owing.

What a cash sale does and does not change

A cash buyer takes away the repair list, the open houses and the wait on someone else's mortgage approval. A tax lien stays put until someone pays it. Whichever way you sell, ask the sheriff's office for the tax status in writing before anything else. Bring your tax tickets, any deed you hold and, for an inherited house, the heir paperwork.

With an inherited house, the homestead exemption may already be gone, so the bill could run higher than what the last owner paid. Settle that with the sheriff before picking a closing date, since a title company will not close over an open ticket.

From first call to closing day

Picture a Raleigh County sale in four stages. Stage one is a call to the sheriff's tax desk at the courthouse for the balance on every ticket attached to the parcel. Stage two is a call to the assessor, since a rental or empty house is taxed at a heavier class than a home its owner lives in. Stage three is gathering papers: tickets, your deed, and any probate or heir documents.

Stage four starts once you accept an offer. A title search turns up liens and open tickets, and whatever it finds is paid out of your proceeds at closing. After that the deed is recorded with the county clerk and the transfer tax is paid. With a cash buyer the stages tend to go faster, since there is no lender adding appraisals or repair demands.

An older house may carry old deed wording and district names like the one noted earlier. Bring those up on day one and the file stays clean, with no surprise close to your closing date.

Frequently asked questions

What are the due dates for Raleigh County tax bills?

One half is due September 1 and the other March 1. Early payment brings a 2.5 percent discount, and each half goes delinquent a month after its due date, on October 1 and April 1.

Where can I pay my Raleigh County tax bill?

Walk in at the courthouse tax office in Beckley (304-255-9162), at the Ghent or Glen Daniel branch, or use the payment link on the sheriff's tax page. The branches shut for lunch from 12:00 to 1:00.

How do I appeal my Raleigh County assessment?

See the assessor while assessments are open for inspection, then take any correction to the commission's review board before it closes in late February. Missing that session waives the correction for the year.

Can a Raleigh County house with delinquent taxes still be sold?

Yes. The balance is paid from your proceeds or ahead of closing, and the title company can confirm the parcel is not on the list of delinquent liens certified to the Auditor each October 31.

Who pays the transfer tax on a Raleigh County sale?

Sellers do, as grantors, unless a buyer agrees to take the deed with the tax still owing. The basic charges are $1.10 plus 55 cents per $500 of value, with a $20 fee added, and a higher county rate is possible.

Cabell County at a glance

Huntington, on the Ohio River in West Virginia's southwest corner, is the seat of Cabell County. Census takers counted 94,350 people in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 91,183. Of its 46,125 housing units, 13.5 percent were vacant, and 39.5 percent of occupied units were rented. Median home value is $129,000.

That mix of owner-occupied homes and rentals shapes the tax bill. Landlords with Class 3 or Class 4 rental property pay a higher rate than owner-occupants, which raises the carrying cost of a vacant unit. If you inherited a house in Huntington or Barboursville and live elsewhere, make sure the sheriff has your current mailing address, because tickets are mailed.

The county also uses its old district names and boundaries as tax and assessment districts, even though county government now runs five numbered magisterial districts. The district appears on your tax ticket, so know which one your parcel falls in.

2026 levy rates

For 2026 the Cabell County Assessor lists levy rates from 1.35520 to 3.46040 per $100 of assessed value, depending on class and location.

Class 2 covers owner-occupied homes and farms. Class 3 holds everything else outside town limits, while Class 4 holds everything else inside them. A landlord in Huntington therefore pays double the Class 2 rate on the same house, because the rental is Class 4.

How the bill is calculated

The bill equals the assessed value times the levy rate per $100. Assessed value is set at 60 percent of market value as of the July 1 assessment date (Code 11-3-1). Exemptions or special levies can change the final number on a real ticket.

Setting rates is not the assessor's job. The levying bodies do that, and the assessor only puts a value on each parcel. The assessor's office offers a tax estimator on its website, so an owner can test a scenario before putting a house on the market.

Where the money goes

Schools take the largest share of Cabell County property tax, roughly 62 percent of the $111.7 million levied on all property for the 2024 tax year. The county government comes next, and municipalities and the state take smaller slices.

School excess levies have been a live topic. In 2023 the Cabell County Board of Education voted to stop funding parks and libraries from excess levy money. A circuit court blocked the move, and the state Supreme Court of Appeals sided with the board in February 2024. Check with the sheriff's office on which levies sit on your district before you tell a buyer what the yearly bill runs.

How to appeal your assessment

Your first stop is the County Commission, which doubles as the Board of Equalization and Review and has to convene by February 1. The assessor's number during that stretch is (304) 526-9800.

The board can wrap up any time after February 15 and must be done by the last day of February. Before it bumps your value up, you are owed five days of written notice. Owners who never appear lose the chance to contest that year's list, with one exception: a petition to the Office of Tax Appeals. In either forum you have to show your case is more likely right than wrong.

  • Pull together nearby sales of similar houses, plus contractor quotes for any condition problems.
  • Check the assessor's record for the wrong square footage, a demolished outbuilding or an incorrect class.
  • To contest a board order, file with the Office of Tax Appeals by March 31 of the tax year.

Due dates and penalties

Bills are mailed starting July 15. Half comes due September 1 and the other half March 1, and a 2.5 percent discount rewards anyone who pays a half ahead of its date.

An unpaid first half turns delinquent October 1, and an unpaid second half April 1. From then on, interest runs at 9 percent a year. The Cabell County Sheriff's Tax Office collects the money at PO Box 2114, Huntington, WV 25721, telephone (304) 526-8672, and runs an online lookup.

Staying delinquent can end in a lien sale. By September 10 the sheriff compiles a second list of overdue land, and liens nobody has redeemed go to the State Auditor on October 31 for public auction. Each listed parcel picks up $25 for the list and $10 per mailed notice. Paying the sheriff before certification clears the parcel.

Homestead exemption and other filing dates

Qualifying owners get the first $20,000 of assessed value knocked off the bill. You can file from July 1 through December 1. Eligibility goes to people 65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled, with two straight years of West Virginia residence.

A few more deadlines worth putting on the calendar at the assessor's office:

  • Farm valuation applications: July 1 to September 1.
  • Business personal property returns: September 1.
  • Personal property returns for everyone else: October 1.

Selling with taxes owed

Whoever held title on July 1 owes that year's tax, and selling the house does not wipe it out. The obligation follows the July 1 owner even if the bill carries another name, so the closing agent usually settles an open ticket out of the seller's proceeds.

With taxes open, the sequence usually goes like this:

  • Ask the sheriff's office for a payoff figure early, because interest at 9 percent per year keeps accruing until the taxes are paid.
  • Pass that payoff to your title agent for the settlement statement.
  • Paying the balance at closing keeps the parcel off a delinquent list.

Landlords selling a rented Huntington house should remember the Class 4 bill is the heavier one, so the payoff can be larger than a neighbor's owner-occupied home of similar size. A cash buyer will take the house with the ticket still open and handle the payoff at the table.

Closing also carries a recording cost. Recording the deed triggers an excise tax of $1.10 per $500 of value, which the county has kept since July 1, 2025. On top of that comes a county tax starting at 55 cents per $500, and the commission may lift it to $1.65. Sellers normally cover both. A $20 clerk fee applies to transfers for consideration.

Flood risk and older homes

Low ground along the Mud River and the Ohio has flooded before, and buyers ask about it. The Mud River's banks have periodically overflowed into the lowlands, and the county's history includes the Ohio River flood of 1937. The state's WV Flood Tool is a place to look up a parcel.

Huntington was laid out in 1871 as the western terminus of the C&O railroad, so parts of the county have housing stock well over a century old. An owner with repairs to make can ask a cash buyer to purchase as-is, which removes the need to fix anything before closing.

September 1. The first half is due September 1, and paying before then earns a 2.5 percent discount. Bills go out starting July 15, and the half goes delinquent October 1.

Yes. Back taxes and interest come out of your proceeds at closing. Get a payoff number from the Sheriff's Tax Office at (304) 526-8672 before you pick a closing date.

Bring your evidence to the Board of Equalization and Review, which is the County Commission in session starting by February 1. A further appeal of its order goes to the Office of Tax Appeals, due March 31.

Berkeley County at a glance

Berkeley County takes up 321.56 square miles of the Shenandoah Valley in West Virginia's Eastern Panhandle, and Martinsburg is its seat. It forms part of the Hagerstown-Martinsburg metropolitan area, and only Kanawha County has more people among the state's 55 counties.

A quick guide to who does what: the Sheriff's Tax Office answers balance questions. The assessor holds the property record and is the contact for value questions. Calling the right number first saves a round of transfers when you are short on time.

One more habit helps: when a buyer's agent or the title company asks a tax question, answer from the paper you were given, not from memory. The ticket, the assessor's notice and the HOA statement each show a figure that someone will verify, and quoting them directly keeps a closing from stalling over a small mismatch.

How the state assesses property

Berkeley County's assessor decides value, and its sheriff sends bills and collects. Each July 1 fixes a parcel's owner, use and worth for the next calendar tax year. The levying bodies are the county board of education, the county commission, municipalities and the State.

Under the constitution, each parcel is sorted into one of four classes:

  • Class I: intangibles and some farm personal property, currently untaxed.
  • Class II: an owner's own residence, used for nothing else, plus farmland in agricultural use.
  • Class III: all other property outside a municipality.
  • Class IV: all other property inside a municipality.

Suppose an investor buys your house and rents it out. The house leaves Class II, and the tax can shift after the sale.

How to protest an assessment

Protests are heard by the county commission, sitting as the board of equalization and review. The sessions run from February 1 to February 28 at the latest, and you must file before that year's taxes fall due. To prepare:

  • Proof of value can be an independent appraisal or contractor repair estimates.
  • Look for errors in the assessor's record on square footage, bedrooms or condition.
  • Find out from the assessor's office how filing works. The commission meets at 400 West Stephen Street, Suite 106, Martinsburg.
  • Disputes over classification or taxability may go to the Tax Commissioner (West Virginia Code 11-3-24a), who rules by the end of February.

The state sends a notice when an assessed value rises. A higher number changes what the buyer will owe, so read yours before closing.

Due dates and homestead exemption

Your ticket arrives from the sheriff on or after July 15. Half comes due September 1 and half March 1. A discount rewards paying early. Interest starts when a half goes delinquent, October 1 for the first and April 1 for the second.

December 1 is the last day to apply for the homestead exemption. West Virginia Code 11-6B-3 exempts $20,000 of assessed value, the first slice, for an owner who is 65 or older or certified permanently and totally disabled, and who lived in West Virginia for the two consecutive calendar years before the tax year. Drawing a similar exemption in another state disqualifies you here.

For a balance, phone the Sheriff's Tax Office at (304) 264-1982. The County Assessor's number is 304-264-1904. Confirm any date with the office before you rely on it.

  • An HOA property with dues unpaid.

Each has an obvious first move. Dues owed to an HOA: request the balance in writing. Taxes: the Sheriff's Tax Office has the figure. An inherited house: assemble the death certificate and court papers. Nothing here is legal or tax advice. It is general information, so verify specifics with the county office or a qualified professional.

Timeline for listing or selling for cash

Settle the tax picture first, because it touches every later step. Learn the balance and which half it covers. Next, gather the HOA statement if you have an HOA, plus any papers an heir will need. Then pick listing or a cash sale to suit your calendar. Listing brings showings, inspection requests and a wait on the buyer's lender. A cash sale brings title work and a closing date you set.

Until when can I protest my assessment?

Through February, ahead of the tax due date. The commission opens its board sessions February 1 and closes them by February 28, and a protest filed after that year's taxes are due is too late.

The first half is due September 1 and the second March 1, once tickets are issued from July 15. Late halves are delinquent after October 1 and April 1 respectively.

Greenbrier County overview

Lewisburg anchors Greenbrier County, a large mountain county in southeastern West Virginia. The 2025 population estimate is 31,578, down 4.3 percent from 32,985 at the 2020 census. Median home value is $128,900 and 72.7 percent of homes are owner-occupied. Nearly one housing unit in five, 19.1 percent of 17,807, stood empty in 2020, so buyers have choices and a seller should price with that in mind.

Three magisterial districts (Eastern, Western and Central) replaced ten older ones in the 1990s. The ten historic names, such as Anthony's Creek, Blue Sulphur and Meadow Bluff, still serve as tax districts, and the one for your parcel is printed on the ticket.

Tax calendar

The assessor's office runs a calendar from July 1 through April 30.

DateWhat happens

Hearings in February are by appointment only. If you want one, call the assessor in January rather than arriving unannounced.

How the assessor values a house

July 1 is the appraisal date for every parcel. The assessor has to inspect each piece of real estate at least once in three years, though values are meant to move with the market every year. The land and personal property books are due to be finished by January 30 and handed to the Board of Equalization and Review by February 1.

By March 3 the assessor certifies the assessed values to the city and town recorders, the school board, the State Board of Education and the county commission. Those bodies lay their rates from the values, and the sheriff prints tickets from the certified rates. In the office's own words, assessors determine values while the levies set by the bodies determine revenue.

State law sets assessed value at 60 percent of true and actual value, defined as the price a property would bring if voluntarily offered for sale. A forced-sale price is off the table.

How to pay

What happens to a delinquent parcel?

The sheriff publishes a delinquent list, and a parcel on it can wind up at a lien auction held through the State Auditor. A second list of land still delinquent on September 1 is prepared by September 10, and liens nobody has redeemed are certified to the Auditor on October 31.

Costs of selling

Taxes for the year belong to whoever owned the property on July 1, and the deed carries a transfer tax. A county with a farmland protection program may add a further transfer tax of up to $1.10 per $500 under a separate statute. Greenbrier has a Farmland Protection Board among its agencies, so ask the county clerk whether the extra tax applies to your sale.

Before listing, collect the payoff from the Sheriff's Tax Office, confirm the district and class with the assessor, and hand both to the title agent.

Inherited and flood-affected homes

These sales can take longer because an estate or a flood history adds steps. The county lists an Estate Services office and estate forms among its agencies, which is where to start when an owner has died and a deed must eventually be signed.

A deadly flood in 2016 along the Meadow River devastated Rupert and Rainelle, and Howard Creek ran through White Sulphur Springs and the Greenbrier grounds. A seller near those waterways should expect questions about repairs. An as-is cash sale skips the repair negotiation.

Selling with a tax balance, step by step

A seller who owes tax has a short list of jobs. First, ask the Sheriff's Tax Office on (304) 647-6609 what is open for each year, because delinquent real estate has to be paid by cashier's check, money order, certified check or cash. Second, tell the title agent which half is paid so the year's tax can be divided correctly at closing. Third, make sure the sheriff has a mailing address that works, since a missed notice carries real consequences.

If the house also needs work or has heirs who disagree, a cash buyer can often close without repairs, and the payoff is settled at the table. That route is worth weighing when a parcel is nearing the September 10 list.

Owners 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, can claim a $20,000 reduction in assessed value, with applications due to the assessor by December 1. At the Sheriff's Tax Office, 912 Court Street North, Suite 3, Lewisburg, or by mail to PO Box 347, Lewisburg, WV 24901. Card payments online add a 2.95 percent fee with a $2.00 minimum.

What is the last day to pay Greenbrier County taxes without penalty?

April 30 is the last day without penalty on the county calendar. The second half still turns delinquent April 1 under state law, and 9 percent interest runs from that date.

Can I appeal my Greenbrier County assessment?

Yes. Value appeals to the assessor wrap up by January 31, then the Board of Equalization and Review hears cases in February by appointment. Beyond that, the Office of Tax Appeals takes over.

Does a Greenbrier County seller owe the tax for the whole year?

Whoever owns the parcel on July 1 is liable for that year's taxes. In practice the closing agent pays any open balance out of the seller's proceeds.

Submit an application to the assessor on or before December 1. Applicants need to be 65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled, and to have lived in West Virginia two years running.

Your venue is the County Commission wearing its Board of Equalization and Review hat, which convenes beginning February 1. Houses are valued as of July 1 at 60 percent of true and actual value, which means the real argument is what yours would have fetched on that day.

Everything else is Class III outside a municipality or Class IV inside one. Hancock County's municipalities are Chester, New Cumberland and Weirton. Class III and IV property is taxed at double the Class II rate, and Class IV also bears the municipal levy.

The assessor's office and filing dates

Wood County at a glance

Wood County lies where the Ohio and Little Kanawha rivers meet, with Parkersburg as the seat. It covers 377 square miles, and the Little Kanawha splits it almost evenly into northern and southern halves. Interstate 77 divides east from west. Most people live west of the interstate in Parkersburg, Vienna, Williamstown and North Hills, the four incorporated communities. The eastern side is rural and includes Mountwood Park, beside the old oil boom town of Volcano.

The county peaked at 93,648 people in the 1980s, counted 84,300 in 2020 and is estimated at 82,385 for 2025. Health care, federal government work, schools, chemicals and manufacturing lead local employment. WVU Medicine Camden Clark Medical Center, the Bureau of the Fiscal Service and Wood County Schools top the list.

Where a house sits decides its property class. Inside a municipality it is Class IV unless it is an owner-occupied home, which is Class II. Outside the four towns, property the owner does not live in is Class III. Class and levy district together shape the rate on your ticket.

Flood history and the floodplain

Floods struck nearly every year until Parkersburg finished its floodwall in 1950 and locks and dams went in on the Ohio, including one at Belleville. A house near either river still draws questions about the floodplain from buyers and insurers. The county's building office keeps a floodplain ordinance, an application and an elevation certificate on its page, and the floodplain contact is 304-420-0911.

The state lists totals of $1.00, $1.50 and $2.00 per $100 for Classes II, III and IV, so a rental or vacant house can cost about twice as much to carry as the same house occupied by its owner.

Filing dates and the homestead exemption

The assessor's 2026 filing season runs from July 1, and the dates differ by form. Individuals have until October 1 to file personal property returns, starting July 1. Businesses, along with anyone seeking the farm exemption, must file by September 1. A homestead application is accepted July 1 through December 1 and starts with the next tax year.

Tickets run on the state calendar. Expect yours from July 15 onward, with installments due September 1 and March 1 and a 2.5 percent discount for paying ahead of either. Interest of 9 percent a year starts once the first half is past October 1, or the second half past April 1.

Under the homestead exemption, $20,000 of assessed value drops off the bill for a resident owner aged 65 or over, or certified permanently and totally disabled. If that is you, double-check that the paperwork was filed, since a lapse inflates the bill on the house you are selling.

How to appeal a valuation

Begin with a conversation at the Assessor's Office. Still unhappy? Present your case to the county commissioners, who serve as the Board of Equalization and Review from February 1 until February 28. The board can reduce a value that exceeds 60 percent of true and actual value, and it must give written notice at least five days before raising one.

Losing at the board sends you to the Office of Tax Appeals, where a petition must be in by March 31 of the tax year. Missing the February window waives the right to argue that year's list. A dispute over whether a home is Class II or Class IV is handled separately with the assessor and the Tax Commissioner.

Good evidence is concrete: a recent appraisal, a repair estimate for a damaged structure, or sales of similar homes. If you plan to sell soon, an appeal is often not worth the effort unless the value is clearly wrong, because the new owner will be assessed on the next cycle anyway.

Unpaid tax and a cash sale

The sheriff certifies unpaid real estate tax for sale, and the State Auditor, not the sheriff, now runs the lien sale. The certification deadline is October 31. Call the Sheriff at 304-624-8685 before you assume anything about timing or redemption cost.

A seller who owes tax can often clear it through closing. Your title company requests the payoff and settles it from proceeds. Recording a deed also draws a county excise tax of 55 cents on each $500 of value.

Minerals, mobile homes and property classes

The Assessor's Office keeps separate divisions for mobile homes and for oil, gas and minerals. A mobile home may be assessed through its own desk at 304-624-8517, and oil and gas or mineral matters go to 304-624-8523. The state also runs its own appraisal process for oil and gas royalties.

Before closing, ask both the assessor and the title company if a mineral interest rides with the parcel and is assessed separately. Deeds do not always say, and a buyer will want a clear answer. Cash buyers are generally fine with houses where title questions like this need work, and we check before we make an offer.

West Virginia's four classes matter too. Class II means a home that the owner lives in and uses only as a residence. Property in a municipality that does not qualify, such as a rental house in Clarksburg, falls in Class IV, and property outside a municipality falls in Class III. Those classes have higher regular ceilings than Class II.

Think of the process in four steps. In week one, request the amount due from the sheriff's taxes-due line and ask whether any mobile home or mineral piece is assessed apart from the house. Calling the Assessor's Office early also lets you learn whether you can use a satellite day in your area rather than driving to Clarksburg.

Getting ready to sell

A quick checklist helps before you list. Dial 304-624-8685 to learn what each ticket owes. Then ask the Assessor's Office for the house's class and whether a homestead exemption is on file. Check whether a mobile home or mineral interest has its own assessment. Hand everything to the title company so payoff and deed tax are set well before closing day.

If the taxes are old, the house needs work, or heirs have not agreed, a sale for cash skips much of the waiting. Taxes owed are still paid out of your proceeds by the title company, and repair bills and showings drop away.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Harrison County property tax due dates?

One half is due September 1 and the other March 1, with a 2.5 percent discount for paying early. After October 1 (first half) or April 1 (second half) the unpaid amount is delinquent and gains 9 percent interest yearly.

Where is the Harrison County Sheriff's tax office?

It is at 229 South 3rd Street, Clarksburg, WV 26301, and the phone for taxes due is 304-624-8685. Online payment is also offered.

When can I apply for the homestead exemption in Harrison County?

Filing opens July 1 and closes December 1, and the exemption then takes effect the next tax year. Owners 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, get $20,000 off assessed value.

What is the deadline to appeal a Harrison County assessment?

Protest in person before the county commission acting as the Board of Equalization and Review between February 1 and February 28. Going further to the Office of Tax Appeals requires a March 31 filing.

Can I sell a Harrison County house that has back taxes?

Yes. Ask a title company to pull the payoff on the overdue tax, and it will be paid from your proceeds when the sale closes.
